# Unit 1: Basic Economic Concepts

## Overview
This unit introduces the foundational ideas of **economics**: **scarcity**, **choice**, **opportunity cost**, **production possibilities**, **comparative advantage**, **trade**, and basic **economic systems**. These concepts matter on the AP exam because they appear repeatedly in both multiple-choice and free-response questions as the logic behind later macroeconomic models.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Scarcity** | The condition that **resources are limited** while human wants are unlimited. | Scarcity is the basic reason economics exists; many AP questions begin with trade-offs caused by limited resources. |
| **Factors of Production** | The inputs used to produce goods and services: **land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship**. | Students must identify which resource is changing and how that affects production and economic growth. |
| **Opportunity Cost** | The value of the **next best alternative forgone** when a choice is made. | A frequent AP trap is confusing total cost with opportunity cost; the exam often asks what must be given up. |
| **Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)** | A graph showing the **maximum combinations** of two goods an economy can produce with available resources and technology. | The PPC is central for analyzing **efficiency**, **underutilization**, **growth**, and **trade-offs**. |
| **Efficiency** | Using resources so that maximum output is produced; on a PPC, this means points **on** the curve. | AP questions often ask students to classify points as **efficient**, **inefficient**, or **unattainable**. |
| **Absolute Advantage** | The ability to produce more of a good using the same resources, or the same amount using fewer resources. | Useful, but less important than comparative advantage; AP questions often contrast the two. |
| **Comparative Advantage** | The ability to produce a good at a **lower opportunity cost** than another producer. | One of the most tested concepts in Unit 1 because it explains **specialization** and **gains from trade**. |
| **Economic Systems** | The ways societies organize production and distribution: **market**, **command**, and **mixed** economies. | Students must compare how different systems answer the basic economic questions of **what**, **how**, and **for whom** to produce. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Scarcity] --> B[Choices must be made]
    B --> C[Each choice has an opportunity cost]
    C --> D[PPC shows trade-offs]
    D --> E[Specialization based on comparative advantage]
    E --> F[Trade]
    F --> G[Greater total output and consumption possibilities]
```

### How to read this chain
1. **Scarcity** forces individuals, firms, and governments to make choices.
2. Every choice creates an **opportunity cost**.
3. Those trade-offs can be modeled with the **PPC**.
4. When producers specialize according to **comparative advantage**, total production rises.
5. **Trade** allows parties to consume beyond what they could achieve alone.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Formula** | **What You Must Know** |
|---|---|
| **Opportunity Cost** | $$\text{Opportunity Cost of Good A} = \frac{\text{Good B given up}}{\text{Good A gained}}$$ |
| **Slope of a Linear PPC** | $$\text{Slope} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$ In economics, the slope reflects the **opportunity cost** of moving from one good to another. |
| **Comparative Advantage Rule** | The producer with the **lower opportunity cost** of making a good has the **comparative advantage** in that good. |
| **Absolute Advantage Rule** | The producer that can make **more output** with the same inputs has the **absolute advantage**. |
| **PPC Point Meanings** | **On** the PPC = efficient; **inside** the PPC = inefficient or underutilized resources; **outside** the PPC = unattainable with current resources and technology. |
| **Economic Growth on a PPC** | An increase in resource quantity, resource quality, or technology shifts the PPC **outward**. |
| **Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost** | As more of one good is produced, larger amounts of the other good must be given up, so opportunity cost rises. This creates a **bowed-out PPC**. |
| **Specialization and Trade Rule** | If two parties specialize according to **comparative advantage** and trade at a mutually acceptable rate, **both can gain**. |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **How They Are Related** | **Key Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Scarcity vs. Shortage** | Both involve limited availability. | **Scarcity** is universal and permanent; a **shortage** is temporary and often market-specific. |
| **Absolute Advantage vs. Comparative Advantage** | Both compare producers’ abilities. | **Absolute advantage** compares productivity; **comparative advantage** compares opportunity cost. Trade depends on **comparative advantage**. |
| **Efficiency vs. Inefficiency** | Both refer to resource use relative to the PPC. | **Efficiency** means producing on the PPC; **inefficiency** means producing inside it. |
| **Movement Along PPC vs. Shift of PPC** | Both change production possibilities. | A **movement along** the PPC reflects reallocating existing resources; a **shift** reflects a change in resources or technology. |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Production Possibilities Curve] --> B[Point on curve]
    A --> C[Point inside curve]
    A --> D[Point outside curve]
    B --> E[Efficient production]
    C --> F[Unemployment or underutilization]
    D --> G[Currently unattainable]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps

- **Comparative advantage is not the same as absolute advantage.** A country can have an absolute advantage in both goods and still benefit from trade if opportunity costs differ.
- **Opportunity cost must be calculated using what is given up**, not what is gained. Read production tables carefully.
- A point **inside** the PPC is not “better” because it is safer or more realistic; it represents **inefficiency**.
- A **bowed-out PPC** reflects **increasing opportunity cost**, not constant opportunity cost. A straight-line PPC implies constant opportunity cost.
- **Trade does not require one side to be worse at everything.** Gains from trade come from specialization based on comparative advantage, not from equal productivity.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define **scarcity** and explain why it forces economic choices.
- [ ] Identify the **four factors of production**: **land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship**.
- [ ] Calculate **opportunity cost** from a word problem, table, or PPC.
- [ ] Distinguish between **absolute advantage** and **comparative advantage**.
- [ ] Determine which producer should specialize in which good using **lower opportunity cost**.
- [ ] Interpret a **PPC** by identifying efficient, inefficient, and unattainable points.
- [ ] Explain the difference between a **movement along** a PPC and an **outward or inward shift**.
- [ ] Compare **market**, **command**, and **mixed** economic systems in terms of how they answer basic economic questions.

flashcards.definition: The condition in which limited resources are insufficient to satisfy unlimited human wants, forcing individuals and societies to make choices.
The value of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
A model that shows the maximum combinations of two goods or categories of goods that can be produced with available resources and technology when resources are fully employed.
An outcome in which the mix of output reflects consumer preferences, occurring where the marginal benefit of the last unit equals its marginal cost.
An outcome in which goods and services are produced at the lowest possible cost, using all available resources without waste.

multipleChoice.questionText: A nation can produce either consumer goods or capital goods. If it moves from a point inside its production possibilities curve to a point on the curve, which of the following most likely occurs?
options: Unemployment decreases and productive efficiency increases
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Unemployment decreases and productive efficiency increases

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following best explains why the production possibilities curve is typically bowed outward from the origin?
options: Resources are not equally suited to producing all goods
Consumer preferences change as output rises
Prices of goods are assumed to be constant
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Resources are not equally suited to producing all goods

fillInTheBlank.questionText: On a production possibilities curve, producing more of one good generally requires giving up some of another good because of ______.
A point located inside a production possibilities curve indicates ______.

flashcards.definition: The ability of a producer to make more of a good or service than another producer using the same quantity of resources, or to make the same amount using fewer resources.
The ability of a producer to make a good or service at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
A situation in which individuals, firms, or nations concentrate their resources on producing the goods and services for which they are relatively most efficient.
An economic system in which decisions about production, resource allocation, and prices are made primarily by the government.
An economic system in which households and firms, acting in their own interest, make most production and consumption decisions through voluntary exchange.

multipleChoice.questionText: Country A can produce $$10$$ tons of wheat or $$5$$ tons of steel, while Country B can produce $$8$$ tons of wheat or $$2$$ tons of steel. Which country has the comparative advantage in steel?
options: Country A, because its opportunity cost of steel is lower
Country B, because it can produce wheat more efficiently
Country A, because it has the absolute advantage in both goods
Country B, because trade eliminates opportunity cost
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Country A, because its opportunity cost of steel is lower

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following is most characteristic of a mixed economy?
options: All resources are allocated exclusively through central planning
Private property and markets exist alongside government intervention
Firms are prohibited from seeking profit
Consumers have no role in determining output
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Private property and markets exist alongside government intervention

If one producer can make a good using fewer inputs than another producer, the first producer has ______ in that good.

# Unit 2: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle

## Overview
This unit introduces the main **macroeconomic indicators** economists use to measure the health of an economy: **GDP**, **unemployment**, and **inflation**. For the AP exam, you need to know not only what these indicators measure, but also how to calculate them, interpret them, and connect them to phases of the **business cycle**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** | The total market value of all **final goods and services** produced within a country in a given period | Central measure of output; AP questions often test what counts in GDP and how to calculate it |
| **Nominal GDP vs. Real GDP** | **Nominal GDP** uses current prices; **real GDP** adjusts for price changes using a base year | Important for separating changes in output from changes in prices |
| **Business Cycle** | Fluctuations in real output over time: **expansion**, **peak**, **contraction**, and **trough** | Students must interpret economic conditions and identify phases from data or graphs |
| **Unemployment** | The share of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it | AP often asks students to distinguish among types of unemployment and calculate rates |
| **Types of Unemployment** | **Frictional**, **structural**, and **cyclical** unemployment | Key for explaining causes of unemployment and linking them to business cycle conditions |
| **Inflation** | A sustained increase in the general price level over time | Essential for interpreting purchasing power, price indices, and policy concerns |
| **Consumer Price Index (CPI)** | A price index based on a fixed market basket of consumer goods and services | Used to measure inflation from the consumer perspective; heavily tested in calculations |
| **GDP Deflator** | A price index comparing nominal GDP to real GDP | Useful for measuring inflation across all domestically produced final goods and services |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Expansion] --> B[Peak]
    B --> C[Contraction or Recession]
    C --> D[Trough]
    D --> A

    A --> E[Real GDP rises]
    A --> F[Unemployment falls]
    C --> G[Real GDP falls]
    C --> H[Cyclical unemployment rises]
```

### How the indicators connect
1. During an **expansion**, **real GDP** tends to rise and **cyclical unemployment** tends to fall.
2. At the **peak**, output is near its short-run maximum before growth slows.
3. During a **contraction**, real output falls, and unemployment usually rises.
4. At the **trough**, the economy reaches its lowest point before recovery begins.
5. Meanwhile, **inflation** may rise or fall depending on changes in aggregate demand, costs, and output conditions.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Formula / Rule** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|
| $$GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)$$ | Expenditure approach to GDP: **consumption**, **investment**, **government spending**, and **net exports** |
| $$\text{Real GDP} = \frac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Price Index}} \times 100$$ | Converts nominal output into inflation-adjusted output |
| $$\text{GDP Deflator} = \frac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Real GDP}} \times 100$$ | Measures the overall price level for domestically produced final goods and services |
| $$\text{Inflation Rate} = \frac{\text{CPI in Year 2} - \text{CPI in Year 1}}{\text{CPI in Year 1}} \times 100$$ | Percent change in CPI from one year to the next |
| $$\text{CPI} = \frac{\text{Cost of Market Basket in Current Year}}{\text{Cost of Market Basket in Base Year}} \times 100$$ | Measures consumer prices using a fixed basket |
| $$\text{Unemployment Rate} = \frac{\text{Unemployed}}{\text{Labor Force}} \times 100$$ | Percent of the labor force without a job but actively seeking work |
| $$\text{Labor Force Participation Rate} = \frac{\text{Labor Force}}{\text{Adult Population}} \times 100$$ | Measures the share of adults working or seeking work |

### Must-know rules
- **GDP includes only final goods and services**, not intermediate goods, to avoid **double counting**.
- **GDP counts production within a country’s borders**, regardless of who owns the resources.
- Used goods are **not counted** in GDP, but the value of services involved in their sale may be counted.
- **Transfer payments** are **not included** in GDP because they do not reflect current production.
- **Cyclical unemployment** changes with the business cycle; **frictional** and **structural** unemployment can exist even in a healthy economy.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Comparison** | **CPI** | **GDP Deflator** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What it measures** | Prices of a fixed basket bought by consumers | Prices of all final goods and services produced domestically | Students must know they are both inflation measures, but not identical |
| **Basket type** | Fixed basket | Changing basket based on current production | Explains why the measures can move differently |
| **Includes imports?** | Yes, if consumers buy them | No, because imports are not part of domestic production | Frequent AP distinction |
| **Used for** | Cost of living, inflation from consumer viewpoint | Broad economy-wide price level | Useful when comparing inflation measures |

| **Comparison** | **Nominal GDP** | **Real GDP** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Price basis** | Current year prices | Base year prices | Helps determine whether output actually changed |
| **Affected by inflation?** | Yes | No, adjusted for inflation | Essential for identifying true economic growth |
| **Best for measuring output growth** | No | Yes | AP often asks which measure is better for comparing years |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **nominal GDP** with **real GDP**. If prices rise but output does not, nominal GDP may increase while real GDP stays unchanged.
- Counting **intermediate goods** in GDP. Only **final goods and services** should be included.
- Assuming all unemployment is bad in the same way. **Frictional unemployment** is often natural and can reflect normal job search.
- Forgetting that discouraged workers are **not** counted as unemployed because they are not actively seeking work.
- Mixing up **CPI** and **GDP deflator**: **CPI** includes imported consumer goods, while the **GDP deflator** does not.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can define **GDP** and identify what is and is not included in it.
- [ ] I can use $$GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)$$ to calculate total output.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **nominal GDP** and **real GDP** and explain why **real GDP** is better for measuring growth.
- [ ] I can identify the phases of the **business cycle**: **expansion**, **peak**, **contraction**, and **trough**.
- [ ] I can calculate the **unemployment rate** and explain the difference between **frictional**, **structural**, and **cyclical** unemployment.
- [ ] I can calculate **CPI** and the **inflation rate** using a market basket.
- [ ] I can calculate and interpret the **GDP deflator**.
- [ ] I can compare **CPI** and **GDP deflator** and explain why they may produce different inflation measures.

flashcards.definition: The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period, usually measured annually or quarterly.
An item purchased by its end user and not used as an input in the production of another product during the same period.
A measure of output valued using current-year prices, so changes can reflect both production and price level changes.
A measure of output valued using prices from a base year, allowing comparison of production across time without the effects of inflation.
Recurring fluctuations in overall economic activity characterized by expansions and contractions in real output over time.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which transaction would be included in the calculation of current-year GDP?
options: The purchase of 100 shares of stock in an online brokerage account
A used car sold by one household to another
A bakery's purchase of flour to make bread sold this year
A newly produced machine purchased by a domestic firm
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: A newly produced machine purchased by a domestic firm

multipleChoice.questionText: If nominal GDP increased by $$8\%$$ while the overall price level increased by $$3\%$$, which of the following is the best approximation of the growth rate of real GDP?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: Using the expenditure approach, GDP is calculated as $$C + I + G + (X - M)$$, where $$I$$ represents ______.
When real GDP falls for a period of time and unemployment tends to rise, the economy is most likely in the ______ phase of the business cycle.

flashcards.definition: Short-term joblessness that occurs when workers are between jobs or are searching for positions that better match their skills and preferences.
Joblessness caused by a mismatch between workers' skills or locations and the needs of employers, often due to technological change or shifts in demand.
A measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a fixed market basket of goods and services.

multipleChoice.questionText: A worker loses a job in coal mining because electric utilities shift permanently toward renewable energy sources, and the worker's skills are not easily transferable. This worker is best classified as experiencing
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: structural unemployment

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following explains why the GDP deflator can differ from the CPI?
options: The GDP deflator includes imports, while the CPI excludes them
The CPI uses only current-year quantities, while the GDP deflator uses only base-year quantities
The GDP deflator measures prices of domestically produced final goods and services, while the CPI includes imported consumer goods
The CPI excludes services, while the GDP deflator includes services
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The GDP deflator measures prices of domestically produced final goods and services, while the CPI includes imported consumer goods

If nominal GDP is $$\$600$$ billion and real GDP is $$\$500$$ billion, then the GDP deflator is ______.

# Unit 3: National Income and Price Determination

## Overview
This unit explains how **aggregate demand** and **aggregate supply** determine the economy’s **price level** and **real output** in the short run and long run. It is essential for the AP exam because students must analyze **shifts in AD/AS**, identify **recessionary** and **inflationary gaps**, and evaluate how **fiscal policy** and the **multiplier effect** change equilibrium.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Aggregate Demand (AD)** | The total demand for a nation’s goods and services at different price levels: $$AD = C + I + G + (X - M)$$ | You must know why AD slopes downward and what causes AD to shift. |
| **Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)** | Output firms will produce at different price levels when some input prices are sticky | AP questions often test SRAS shifts from input costs, productivity, or expectations. |
| **Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS)** | The economy’s full-employment output, or **potential output** | Critical for identifying whether the economy has a **gap** and for long-run adjustment. |
| **Equilibrium Price Level and Real GDP** | The intersection of **AD** and **SRAS** | This determines short-run macroeconomic equilibrium and is central to graph analysis. |
| **Recessionary Gap** | When equilibrium real GDP is below full-employment GDP | Students must connect this to unemployment, deflationary pressure, and expansionary policy. |
| **Inflationary Gap** | When equilibrium real GDP exceeds full-employment GDP | Often tested with demand-pull inflation and contractionary policy responses. |
| **Multiplier Effect** | The idea that an initial change in spending causes a larger change in real GDP | Frequently appears in fiscal policy multiple-choice and FRQ calculations. |
| **Automatic Stabilizers** | Government programs and tax structures that automatically reduce fluctuations | Important for distinguishing automatic from discretionary fiscal policy. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Change in spending or costs] --> B[Shift in AD or SRAS]
    B --> C[New short-run equilibrium]
    C --> D[Change in real GDP]
    C --> E[Change in price level]
    D --> F["Possible output gap (recessionary or inflationary)"]
    F --> G[Pressure on wages and resource prices]
    G --> H[Shift in SRAS toward LRAS]
    H --> I[Long-run equilibrium at full-employment output]
```

### Fiscal policy transmission
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Government changes taxes or spending] --> B[Change in disposable income or direct spending]
    B --> C[Change in consumption or aggregate demand]
    C --> D[Multiplier effect]
    D --> E[Change in real GDP and price level]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Formula / Rule** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|
| $$GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)$$ | Basic expenditure approach; on AP Macro, this also helps define **AD**. |
| $$AD = C + I + G + (X - M)$$ | Total planned spending at each price level. |
| $$MPC = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta Y_d}$$ | **Marginal propensity to consume**: fraction of extra disposable income spent. |
| $$MPS = \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta Y_d}$$ | **Marginal propensity to save**: fraction of extra disposable income saved. |
| $$MPC + MPS = 1$$ | Key relationship used in multiplier problems. |
| $$\text{Spending Multiplier} = \frac{1}{1 - MPC} = \frac{1}{MPS}$$ | Used for changes in **government spending**, **investment**, or other autonomous spending. |
| $$\text{Tax Multiplier} = \frac{-MPC}{1 - MPC}$$ | Tax changes have a smaller effect than equal-sized spending changes. |
| **Recessionary gap** | Occurs when equilibrium output is **less than** full-employment output. |
| **Inflationary gap** | Occurs when equilibrium output is **greater than** full-employment output. |
| **Long-run adjustment rule** | If output is below LRAS, nominal wages and input prices tend to fall, shifting **SRAS right**. If output is above LRAS, nominal wages and input prices tend to rise, shifting **SRAS left**. |

### Must-know shift rules
- **AD shifts right** when **consumption**, **investment**, **government spending**, or **net exports** rise.
- **AD shifts left** when those components fall.
- **SRAS shifts right** with lower input costs, higher productivity, or lower business taxes.
- **SRAS shifts left** with higher input costs, supply shocks, or lower productivity.
- **LRAS** changes only when the economy’s productive capacity changes, such as with labor force growth, capital growth, or technology.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Comparison** | **Aggregate Demand** | **Short-Run Aggregate Supply** | **Long-Run Aggregate Supply** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What shifts it?** | Changes in $$C, I, G, X, M$$ | Input prices, productivity, business taxes | Quantity/quality of resources, technology, institutions |
| **Why does it matter?** | Changes spending in the economy | Changes production costs in the short run | Shows **full-employment output** |
| **Typical AP result of rightward shift** | Higher real GDP and higher price level | Higher real GDP and lower price level | More potential output |
| **Typical AP result of leftward shift** | Lower real GDP and lower price level | Lower real GDP and higher price level | Less potential output |

### Fiscal policy comparison

| **Policy Type** | **Tool** | **Used For** | **Likely Effect on AD** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Expansionary fiscal policy** | Increase $$G$$ or decrease taxes | Close a **recessionary gap** | **AD shifts right** |
| **Contractionary fiscal policy** | Decrease $$G$$ or increase taxes | Close an **inflationary gap** | **AD shifts left** |
| **Automatic stabilizers** | Progressive taxes, unemployment benefits | Smooth fluctuations without new legislation | Reduce the size of AD swings |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing a **movement along AD** with a **shift of AD**. A change in the **price level** causes movement along the curve; a change in **$$C, I, G, \text{or } (X-M)$$** shifts it.
- Assuming **LRAS** shifts whenever **AD** shifts. **AD** changes short-run equilibrium, but **LRAS** only changes when productive capacity changes.
- Forgetting that the **tax multiplier** is **smaller in magnitude** than the **spending multiplier**.
- Mixing up **recessionary gap** and **inflationary gap**. Below full-employment GDP means recessionary; above it means inflationary.
- Treating **automatic stabilizers** as **discretionary fiscal policy**. Automatic stabilizers work without a new law being passed.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can define **aggregate demand**, **SRAS**, and **LRAS**.
- [ ] I can explain why **AD** slopes downward and what causes it to shift.
- [ ] I can identify factors that shift **SRAS** versus factors that shift **LRAS**.
- [ ] I can determine equilibrium **real GDP** and **price level** from an **AD-AS** graph.
- [ ] I can identify a **recessionary gap** or **inflationary gap** relative to **LRAS**.
- [ ] I can calculate and apply the **spending multiplier** and **tax multiplier**.
- [ ] I can explain how **expansionary** and **contractionary fiscal policy** affect **AD**.
- [ ] I can describe how **automatic stabilizers** reduce business cycle fluctuations.
- [ ] I can explain how the economy self-adjusts from a short-run gap back to **long-run equilibrium**.

flashcards.definition: The total quantity of domestically produced final goods and services that households, firms, government, and foreign buyers are willing and able to purchase at different overall price levels.
The relationship showing the quantity of real output firms will produce at different overall price levels when some input prices, especially nominal wages, are slow to adjust.
The vertical relationship showing the economy's full-employment real output, determined by available resources, technology, and institutions rather than the overall price level.
The relationship between disposable income and household spending, indicating how much spending changes when after-tax income changes.
The fraction of an additional dollar of disposable income that households spend on consumption rather than save.

multipleChoice.questionText: If households become more optimistic about future income and employment, which immediate macroeconomic effect is most likely in the United States, assuming no change in price level?
options: Aggregate demand shifts right because consumption spending increases.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because nominal wages fall.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts right because potential output rises immediately.
Aggregate demand shifts left because saving automatically rises more than consumption.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Aggregate demand shifts right because consumption spending increases.

multipleChoice.questionText: An economy is initially in long-run equilibrium. A sharp increase in input prices reduces firms' profitability at each price level. In the short run, this change will most likely cause which combination of effects?
options: A leftward shift of short-run aggregate supply, higher price level, and lower real output
A rightward shift of aggregate demand, lower price level, and higher real output
A rightward shift of long-run aggregate supply, higher real output, and no change in price level
A leftward shift of aggregate demand, lower price level, and lower real output
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: A leftward shift of short-run aggregate supply, higher price level, and lower real output

fillInTheBlank.questionText: In the simple spending model, the spending multiplier equals $$\frac{1}{1-MPC}$$, so if the marginal propensity to consume is $$0.8$$, the multiplier is ______.
A decrease in the overall price level increases the purchasing power of money balances and tends to raise consumption spending; this is known as the ______ effect.

flashcards.definition: The ratio of the total change in real GDP to an initial change in autonomous spending, arising because one person's spending becomes another person's income.
The amount by which equilibrium real output falls short of the full-employment level, creating cyclical unemployment and downward pressure on prices over time.
The amount by which equilibrium real output exceeds the full-employment level, creating upward pressure on prices and wages over time.
Features of the fiscal system that change government spending or tax collections without new legislation, reducing fluctuations in real GDP over the business cycle.
A reduction in private investment caused by higher interest rates when government borrowing increases the demand for loanable funds.

multipleChoice.questionText: Suppose the economy is in a recessionary gap and the government increases spending by $$\$40$$ billion. If the marginal propensity to consume is $$0.75$$ and there is no crowding out, what is the maximum predicted change in real GDP?
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: $$\$160$$ billion

multipleChoice.questionText: Which policy change best illustrates an automatic stabilizer operating during an economic downturn?
options: Congress passes a new infrastructure bill after lengthy debate.
Tax revenues fall and unemployment benefit payments rise as incomes decline.
The central bank sells government securities to reduce inflationary pressure.
Firms cut nominal wages to restore full employment output.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Tax revenues fall and unemployment benefit payments rise as incomes decline.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: When equilibrium real GDP exceeds full-employment output, the economy has an ______ gap.
Expansionary fiscal policy intended to close a recessionary gap would most directly involve increasing government spending or ______ taxes.

# Unit 4: Financial Sector

## Overview
This unit explains how **money**, **banks**, and the **Federal Reserve** interact to influence the economy. For the AP exam, you must understand how the **money supply** is measured and created, how **monetary policy tools** shift interest rates, and how to analyze outcomes in the **money market** and **loanable funds market**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Money** | Any asset that serves as a **medium of exchange**, **unit of account**, and **store of value** | AP questions often test whether something qualifies as money and whether it performs money’s three functions |
| **Money Supply** | The total amount of liquid financial assets in the economy, especially **$$M_1$$** and **$$M_2$$** | You may need to identify what counts in each measure and connect changes in money supply to interest rates |
| **Fractional Reserve Banking** | A banking system in which banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest | Central to understanding **money creation** and the **money multiplier** |
| **Required Reserve Ratio** | The fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves | Determines how much lending banks can do and affects the maximum expansion of the money supply |
| **Money Multiplier** | The maximum amount the banking system can expand deposits from an initial change in reserves | Frequently appears in quantitative AP questions involving reserve requirements and deposit expansion |
| **Federal Reserve** | The central bank of the United States that regulates banks and conducts **monetary policy** | You must know the Fed’s structure, role, and policy tools |
| **Monetary Policy Tools** | **Open market operations**, **discount rate**, and **reserve requirements** | AP asks how each tool changes reserves, money supply, and interest rates |
| **Money Market and Loanable Funds** | Models showing how the supply and demand for money and borrowing/saving determine interest rates | Essential for graph analysis and for linking policy changes to macro outcomes |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Federal Reserve changes policy tool"] --> B["Bank reserves change"]
    B --> C["Banks change lending"]
    C --> D["Money supply changes"]
    D --> E["Nominal interest rate changes in money market"]
    E --> F["Investment spending changes"]
    F --> G["Aggregate demand changes"]
    G --> H["Real output and price level may change"]

    A2["New deposit enters banking system"] --> B2["Bank keeps required reserves"]
    B2 --> C2["Bank lends excess reserves"]
    C2 --> D2["Loan becomes new deposit in another bank"]
    D2 --> B2
```

### Two essential chains to remember
1. **Money creation process**
   1. A bank receives a deposit.
   2. It holds **required reserves**.
   3. It lends **excess reserves**.
   4. The loan is spent and redeposited elsewhere.
   5. The process repeats, expanding the money supply.

2. **Monetary policy transmission**
   1. The **Fed** changes bank reserves.
   2. This shifts the **money supply**.
   3. Interest rates in the **money market** change.
   4. **Investment** and sometimes **consumption** change.
   5. **Aggregate demand** shifts.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Formula** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|
| $$\text{Required Reserves} = \text{Deposits} \times \text{Required Reserve Ratio}$$ | Minimum reserves a bank must hold |
| $$\text{Excess Reserves} = \text{Actual Reserves} - \text{Required Reserves}$$ | Amount available for new lending |
| $$\text{Simple Money Multiplier} = \frac{1}{\text{Required Reserve Ratio}}$$ | Maximum potential deposit expansion |
| $$\text{Maximum Change in Money Supply} = \text{Excess Reserves} \times \frac{1}{\text{Required Reserve Ratio}}$$ | Used in banking expansion problems |
| **Open market purchase** | Fed buys bonds, increasing bank reserves, increasing money supply, and lowering interest rates |
| **Open market sale** | Fed sells bonds, decreasing bank reserves, decreasing money supply, and raising interest rates |
| **Lower discount rate** | Encourages banks to borrow from the Fed, increasing reserves and money supply |
| **Higher discount rate** | Discourages bank borrowing from the Fed, decreasing reserves and money supply |
| **Lower reserve requirement** | Increases lending ability and increases the money multiplier |
| **Higher reserve requirement** | Reduces lending ability and decreases the money multiplier |

### Money market rules
- **Money demand** slopes downward because at lower interest rates, people prefer to hold more money.
- **Money supply** is typically drawn as **vertical**, set by the Fed.
- If **money supply increases**, the equilibrium interest rate **falls**.
- If **money demand increases**, the equilibrium interest rate **rises**.

### Loanable funds rules
- **Supply of loanable funds** comes mainly from saving.
- **Demand for loanable funds** comes mainly from borrowers, especially firms seeking investment funds and governments borrowing through deficits.
- An increase in the **supply** of loanable funds lowers real interest rates.
- An increase in the **demand** for loanable funds raises real interest rates.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **How They Differ / Connect** | **AP Exam Importance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Money Market vs. Loanable Funds Market** | The **money market** determines the **nominal interest rate** through money supply and money demand. The **loanable funds market** determines the **real interest rate** through saving and borrowing. | Students often confuse which graph to use and what shifts each curve |
| **Expansionary vs. Contractionary Monetary Policy** | **Expansionary** policy increases reserves and money supply to lower interest rates. **Contractionary** policy decreases reserves and money supply to raise interest rates. | Common graphing and policy-identification question type |
| **Required Reserves vs. Excess Reserves** | **Required reserves** must be held; **excess reserves** can be lent out. | Crucial in money creation calculations |
| **Open Market Operations vs. Discount Rate vs. Reserve Requirement** | All affect reserves, but **open market operations** are the Fed’s most commonly used tool because they are flexible and precise. | AP often asks which tool the Fed most often uses |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Expansionary monetary policy"] --> B["Increase bank reserves"]
    B --> C["Increase money supply"]
    C --> D["Lower nominal interest rate"]
    D --> E["Increase investment"]
    E --> F["Increase aggregate demand"]

    G["Contractionary monetary policy"] --> H["Decrease bank reserves"]
    H --> I["Decrease money supply"]
    I --> J["Higher nominal interest rate"]
    J --> K["Decrease investment"]
    K --> L["Decrease aggregate demand"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **money demand** with **demand for bonds** or **demand for loanable funds**. These are not the same graph or concept.
- Forgetting that the **money market** uses the **nominal interest rate**, while the **loanable funds market** focuses on the **real interest rate**.
- Assuming the **money multiplier** gives the actual change in money supply in all cases. On AP, it is usually a **maximum** or **simple** multiplier unless otherwise specified.
- Mixing up **open market purchases** and **open market sales**. A **purchase** by the Fed is expansionary; a **sale** is contractionary.
- Believing banks can lend all deposits. They can lend only **excess reserves**, not required reserves.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] Define the three functions of **money**: **medium of exchange**, **unit of account**, and **store of value**
- [ ] Distinguish between **$$M_1$$** and **$$M_2$$**
- [ ] Calculate **required reserves**, **excess reserves**, and the **simple money multiplier**
- [ ] Explain how **fractional reserve banking** creates money
- [ ] Identify how each Fed tool changes **bank reserves**, **money supply**, and **interest rates**
- [ ] Draw and interpret the **money market** graph, including shifts in money supply and money demand
- [ ] Draw and interpret the **loanable funds market** graph, including shifts in supply and demand
- [ ] Explain how **expansionary** and **contractionary monetary policy** affect **investment** and **aggregate demand**

# Unit 5: Long-Run Consequences of Stabilization Policies

## Overview
This unit explains how **stabilization policies** affect the economy over time, especially through the **Phillips curve**, **short-run and long-run aggregate supply**, **crowding out**, and competing macroeconomic perspectives. For the AP exam, you must distinguish between **short-run gains** from policy and the **long-run adjustments** that can eliminate those gains while creating inflation, higher interest rates, or changing expectations.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Short-Run Phillips Curve (SRPC)** | A curve showing an inverse relationship between **inflation** and **unemployment** in the short run. | AP questions often ask how demand shocks move the economy **along** the SRPC. |
| **Long-Run Phillips Curve (LRPC)** | A vertical curve at the **natural rate of unemployment**. In the long run, there is no tradeoff between inflation and unemployment. | Essential for showing why expansionary policy cannot permanently reduce unemployment below the natural rate. |
| **Adaptive Expectations** | The idea that people adjust inflation expectations based on past inflation. | Explains why the **SRPC shifts** after repeated inflationary policy. |
| **Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)** | The upward-sloping aggregate supply curve in the short run, when some input prices are sticky. | Needed to analyze short-run output and price level effects of stabilization policy. |
| **Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS)** | The vertical aggregate supply curve at **full-employment output**. | Shows that in the long run, output returns to potential output rather than staying above it. |
| **Crowding Out** | When government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment spending. | Common AP application of **expansionary fiscal policy**, especially when deficits increase. |
| **Monetarist View** | A school of thought emphasizing the role of the **money supply** and arguing that discretionary policy can destabilize the economy. | AP may compare monetarist skepticism to Keynesian support for active stabilization. |
| **Rational Expectations / New Classical View** | The idea that people use all available information to predict policy effects, limiting the real impact of anticipated policy. | Helps explain why some economists think systematic policy may have little effect on real output. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Expansionary policy increases AD"] --> B["Real output rises above potential output"]
    B --> C["Unemployment falls below natural rate"]
    C --> D["Inflation rises"]
    D --> E["Workers and firms adjust inflation expectations"]
    E --> F["SRAS shifts left"]
    F --> G["Output returns to LRAS (full employment)"]
    G --> H["Price level is higher than before"]

    I["Government deficit spending"] --> J["Government demand for loanable funds rises"]
    J --> K["Real interest rate rises"]
    K --> L["Private investment falls"]
    L --> M["Crowding out reduces long-run growth effects"]
```

### What this means
1. In the **short run**, expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can reduce cyclical unemployment.
2. If output rises above **potential output**, the economy enters an **inflationary gap**.
3. Over time, **input costs** and **inflation expectations** rise, shifting **SRAS left**.
4. The economy returns to **full-employment output** in the long run, but at a **higher price level**.
5. With **fiscal policy**, borrowing can raise interest rates and reduce private investment through **crowding out**.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Expression** | **What You Must Know** |
|---|---|
| $$Y_f$$ | **Full-employment output**; the level of output shown by **LRAS**. |
| **SRPC rule** | In the short run, lower unemployment is typically associated with higher inflation. |
| **LRPC rule** | In the long run, unemployment returns to the **natural rate**, so there is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff. |
| $$\text{Real interest rate} = \text{Nominal interest rate} - \text{Expected inflation}$$ | Useful for understanding borrowing, investment, and crowding out. |
| **Crowding out rule** | Expansionary fiscal policy financed by borrowing may increase interest rates and reduce **private investment**. |
| **Long-run adjustment rule** | If actual output exceeds potential output, wages and resource prices rise, causing **SRAS** to shift left until output returns to $$Y_f$$. |
| **Natural rate of unemployment** | The unemployment rate that exists when the economy is at full employment; includes **frictional** and **structural** unemployment, not cyclical unemployment. |
| **Monetarist rule of thumb** | Changes in the **money supply** are a major cause of changes in nominal GDP and inflation over time. |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Comparison** | **Short Run** | **Long Run** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Phillips Curve** | **SRPC** shows a tradeoff between inflation and unemployment. | **LRPC** is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment. | Students must know that the tradeoff is temporary, not permanent. |
| **Aggregate Supply** | **SRAS** can shift because wages and input prices are sticky. | **LRAS** is vertical at potential output. | Explains why policy affects output temporarily but not permanently. |
| **Expansionary Fiscal Policy** | Increases **AD**, raises output and employment. | Can raise price level and cause **crowding out**. | AP often asks for both the short-run benefit and long-run cost. |
| **Keynesian vs. Monetarist / New Classical** | **Keynesians** support active stabilization policy. | **Monetarists** and **new classical economists** worry about lags, expectations, and inflation. | Important for evaluating policy effectiveness, not just graphing it. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Keynesian view"] --> B["Active fiscal and monetary policy can stabilize output"]
    C["Monetarist view"] --> D["Policy lags and money supply instability can worsen fluctuations"]
    E["New Classical / Rational Expectations view"] --> F["Anticipated policy has limited effect on real output"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing a **movement along** the **short-run Phillips curve** with a **shift** of the curve. Demand changes usually cause movement along the SRPC; changing inflation expectations shifts it.
- Assuming policymakers can permanently keep unemployment below the **natural rate**. In the long run, unemployment returns to the natural rate.
- Forgetting that **crowding out** mainly limits the effectiveness of **fiscal policy**, especially when government borrowing raises interest rates.
- Mixing up **SRAS** and **LRAS** adjustment. In the long run, it is **SRAS** that shifts to restore equilibrium at **LRAS**.
- Believing all schools of thought support discretionary stabilization equally. **Keynesian**, **monetarist**, and **new classical** economists differ sharply on policy effectiveness.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] Explain the difference between the **short-run Phillips curve** and the **long-run Phillips curve**.
- [ ] Show how **expansionary policy** can reduce unemployment in the short run.
- [ ] Explain why the economy returns to **full-employment output** in the long run.
- [ ] Describe how rising inflation expectations can shift the **SRPC**.
- [ ] Use **SRAS**, **AD**, and **LRAS** to explain long-run adjustment from an inflationary gap.
- [ ] Explain **crowding out** using the **loanable funds** or interest rate mechanism.
- [ ] Compare **Keynesian**, **monetarist**, and **new classical** views of stabilization policy.
- [ ] Identify why short-run policy success may create long-run costs such as higher inflation or reduced investment.

# Unit 6: Open Economy: International Trade and Finance

## Overview
This unit explains how economies interact through **trade**, **financial flows**, and **exchange rates**. For the AP exam, you need to understand how the **balance of payments**, **foreign exchange market**, and **trade deficits/surpluses** connect to macroeconomic outcomes like **net exports**, **aggregate demand**, and **currency appreciation or depreciation**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Open economy** | An economy that trades goods, services, and financial assets with other countries | AP questions often contrast open and closed economies, especially when analyzing **net exports** and international capital flows |
| **Balance of payments** | A record of all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world | You may need to classify transactions and explain why the accounts must balance overall |
| **Current account** | Tracks trade in **goods and services**, **income flows**, and **transfers** | A **trade deficit** or **surplus** appears here; AP questions often link this to **net exports** |
| **Financial account** | Tracks purchases of **real and financial assets** across countries | Important for understanding how capital inflows and outflows offset current account imbalances |
| **Foreign exchange market** | The market where currencies are bought and sold | Central to questions about **exchange rate determination** using **supply** and **demand** |
| **Exchange rate** | The price of one currency in terms of another | AP students must predict effects of appreciation/depreciation on **imports**, **exports**, and **aggregate demand** |
| **Appreciation / Depreciation** | An **appreciation** raises a currency’s value; a **depreciation** lowers it | Frequently tested because they change **export competitiveness** and **import prices** |
| **Trade deficit / surplus** | A **deficit** means imports exceed exports; a **surplus** means exports exceed imports | Students must connect trade balances to **current account**, **capital inflows**, and macroeconomic performance |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Foreign demand for domestic currency rises] --> B[Demand for currency increases]
    B --> C[Currency appreciates]
    C --> D[Domestic exports become more expensive abroad]
    C --> E[Foreign imports become cheaper domestically]
    D --> F[Exports fall]
    E --> G[Imports rise]
    F --> H[Net exports decrease]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Aggregate demand decreases]

    J[Foreign demand for domestic currency falls] --> K[Demand for currency decreases]
    K --> L[Currency depreciates]
    L --> M[Domestic exports become cheaper abroad]
    L --> N[Foreign imports become more expensive domestically]
    M --> O[Exports rise]
    N --> P[Imports fall]
    O --> Q[Net exports increase]
    P --> Q
    Q --> R[Aggregate demand increases]
```

### How the accounts connect
1. A country that imports more than it exports has a **current account deficit**.
2. That deficit must be matched by a **financial account surplus** because foreign sellers receive funds that are often used to buy domestic assets.
3. In AP terms, the **balance of payments** balances because international transactions are recorded twice: once as a payment and once as a receipt.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Formula** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|
| $$GDP = C + I + G + X_n$$ | In an open economy, **net exports** are part of aggregate expenditure |
| $$X_n = X - M$$ | **Net exports** equal **exports minus imports** |
| **Current account** includes **goods, services, income, and transfers** | Know what belongs here versus the financial account |
| **Financial account** includes purchases of **stocks, bonds, real estate, businesses, and other assets** | AP often asks where capital inflows and outflows are recorded |
| $$\text{Current Account} + \text{Financial Account} \approx 0$$ | In simplified AP treatment, deficits in one account are offset by surpluses in the other |
| **Currency appreciation** | A stronger currency makes **imports cheaper** and **exports more expensive** |
| **Currency depreciation** | A weaker currency makes **exports cheaper** and **imports more expensive** |
| **Demand for a currency** comes from foreigners wanting that country’s **goods, services, or assets** | Helps explain shifts in the foreign exchange market |
| **Supply of a currency** comes from residents wanting **foreign goods, services, or assets** | Helps explain why imports and capital outflows affect exchange rates |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Key Difference / Connection** | **AP Exam Significance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Current account** vs. **Financial account** | The current account records trade-related flows; the financial account records asset purchases | A current account deficit is typically paired with a financial account surplus |
| **Appreciation** vs. **Depreciation** | Appreciation raises currency value; depreciation lowers it | Students must predict the effect on **exports**, **imports**, and **net exports** |
| **Trade deficit** vs. **Trade surplus** | Deficit: $$M > X$$. Surplus: $$X > M$$ | You may need to connect these to **aggregate demand** and international borrowing/lending |
| **Demand for currency** vs. **Supply of currency** | Demand comes from foreigners buying domestic products/assets; supply comes from domestic buyers seeking foreign products/assets | Useful for graphing exchange rate changes in the **FOREX market** |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Higher domestic interest rates] --> B[Foreign investors buy domestic assets]
    B --> C[Demand for domestic currency rises]
    C --> D[Currency appreciates]
    D --> E[Net exports fall]

    F[Lower domestic interest rates] --> G[Foreign investors buy fewer domestic assets]
    G --> H[Demand for domestic currency falls]
    H --> I[Currency depreciates]
    I --> J[Net exports rise]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- **Do not confuse** the **current account** with the **financial account**. Trade in goods and services goes in the current account; purchases of assets go in the financial account.
- A **trade deficit** is **not automatically “bad”** in AP analysis. It may reflect strong domestic income, high demand for imports, or capital inflows.
- **Appreciation** hurts **net exports**, while **depreciation** helps **net exports**. Students often reverse this.
- In the foreign exchange market, demand for a currency rises when foreigners want that country’s **exports** or **assets**—not when domestic consumers want imports.
- Remember the AP simplification: if one major account is negative, the other tends to be positive so the overall **balance of payments** balances.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] Define an **open economy** and explain how it differs from a closed economy.
- [ ] Calculate **net exports** using $$X_n = X - M$$.
- [ ] Identify whether a transaction belongs in the **current account** or **financial account**.
- [ ] Explain why a **current account deficit** is offset by a **financial account surplus**.
- [ ] Use **supply** and **demand** to explain exchange rate changes in the **foreign exchange market**.
- [ ] Predict how **currency appreciation** affects **exports**, **imports**, and **aggregate demand**.
- [ ] Predict how **currency depreciation** affects **exports**, **imports**, and **aggregate demand**.
- [ ] Connect changes in **interest rates** or capital flows to changes in **currency value** and **net exports**.

The demand for euros in foreign exchange markets decreases because U.S. tourists stop traveling abroad.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: U.S. goods become more expensive to Europeans, decreasing U.S. net exports.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following would most likely increase the demand for the Mexican peso in the foreign exchange market?
options: Mexican inflation rises relative to inflation in the United States.
U.S. investors increase purchases of Mexican government bonds.
Mexico imposes strict limits on foreign investment inflows.
Mexican households increase imports of U.S. consumer goods.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: U.S. investors increase purchases of Mexican government bonds.
